King Rudolph swiped his hand in the air. “I’ll invite all the priests, every nobleman, and every bishop in my empire, from Vienna to Frankfurt. They’ll see. When you win, all of them will know that Rudolph is no fool.”

The Maharal spoke slowly, clearly, and in perfect Latin, as he answered every one of the challenges posed by the cardinals. There was pin-drop silence as his

voice echoed off the tall cream- and-gold ceilings.

One cardinal paced nervously as he issued a response. The Maharal issued a strong retort; the cardinal turned red. Indignant murmurs began to ripple through the crowd.

When the Maharal finally stepped off the stage, his head was bowed low, and his face was pensive. It was clear that he’d won the debate—and that was precisely the problem.

Perel pressed a Tehillim against her chest as she watched her husband close his satchel and tie it around his shoulder. Packed inside was the bread and cheese which she had prepared, the vegetables and grains, his long black frock, his tallis, tefillin, and siddur, and of course, his precious manuscripts.
